title: Physics-Informed Fusion-MIONet with IFENN: A Generalized Framework for Coupled Poroelasticity Problems
authors: Fouad M. Amin, Rigoberto Moncada, Panos Pantidis, Diab W. Abueidda, Fan Fei, Mostafa E. Mobasher
abstract: Complex, high-dimensional, large-scale poroelasticity simulations using traditional numerical solvers can be prohibitively expensive in terms of computational resources. We introduce an innovative framework for poroelasticity problems that integrates physics-informed machine learning (PI-ML) models with high-performance FEM solvers. This integration is achieved through the Integrated Finite Element Neural Network (IFENN) setup, which uses a staggered scheme between an FEM solver for mechanical equilibrium and a PI-ML model for fluid-flow predictions. We introduce a novel Physics-Informed Fusion-MIONet (PIF-MIONet) architecture, in which a fusion network encodes the outputs of the MIONet branches. The MIONet encodes different input functions, and the fusion network enables early interaction between the inputs, supporting generalization across multiple scenarios while adhering to the underlying physics of the poroelasticity problem. We study different examples, covering 2D and 3D domains and considering variable material properties and time discretizations. We test the models on unseen loading histories, demonstrating accuracy and generalizability across scenarios. For complex geometries and boundary conditions, we show that with both physics and data considered in the loss function, a PI-ML model can be trained using only 0.1\% of the training increments used for pure data-driven training. In addition, we expand the PIF-MIONet to incorporate a domain decomposition approach, which was found to be particularly useful when modeling flow over more complex geometries with more localized phenomena. For the first time, IFENN is implemented using the open-source multiphysics simulator GEOS for the FEM part, providing a path for the framework's application to industrial-scale simulations and complex multiphysics problems.

infographic.key_insight: PIF-MIONet couples physics-informed fluid-flow predictions with FEM mechanical equilibrium through IFENN to model poroelasticity across varying inputs.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Integration with the open-source GEOS simulator offers a path toward accelerating complex, industrial-scale coupled poromechanics simulations.
method: Stagger FEM mechanical-equilibrium solves with neural fluid-flow predictions.
Fuse MIONet branch outputs to enable early interaction among input functions.
Use physics-and-data training and extend the architecture with domain decomposition for localized flow.
infographic.evidence_signal: Tests span 2D and 3D domains, variable material properties and time discretizations, and unseen loading histories; for complex cases, physics-and-data training used only 0.1% of the training increments used for pure data-driven training.
infographic.watch_item: Industrial-scale speedups and robustness of the staggered coupling are not quantified in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Physics-Informed Fusion-MIONet with IFENN: A Generalized Framework for Coupled Poroelasticity Problems

title: Convergence and error analysis of problem-independent machine learning (PIML) with linear completeness
authors: Ke Tan, Chong-Jun Li, Xu Guo
abstract: Problem-independent machine learning (PIML) is an effective computational approach that combines the finite element method with machine learning. PIML uses neural networks to learn the mapping from material distributions or element geometries to the numerical shape functions of substructures. This approach avoids repeated computation while preserving the conformity of the underlying finite element discretization, thereby significantly improving the efficiency of substructure-based finite element analysis. However, existing studies on PIML have primarily focused on numerical accuracy and computational efficiency, while rigorous theoretical analyses of its approximation errors are still limited. In this paper, we establish an error analysis framework for PIML from a classical finite element perspective, in which the numerical error is bounded in terms of the finite element discretization error and the network generalization error. Our analysis shows that, when only rigid-body displacement invariance is enforced, the resulting error estimate contains a learning-induced term that does not necessarily decrease under mesh refinement. To ensure convergence, we propose an improved PIML scheme with linear completeness. By using linear displacement field constraints to reconstruct the corresponding columns of the transition matrix, we ensure that the resulting numerical shape-function space contains the space of linear polynomials. We derive error estimates and establish convergence results of the improved scheme in the H1 and L2 norms. Numerical experiments verify the theoretical results and demonstrate that the improved PIML achieves optimal convergence rates, good generalization performance, and numerical stability.

infographic.key_insight: Enforcing linear completeness in PIML removes a barrier to mesh-refinement convergence and enables rigorous H1- and L2-norm error estimates.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach accelerates substructure-based finite element analysis by learning reusable numerical shape functions while preserving conformity and convergence.
method: Learn material-distribution or element-geometry mappings to substructure shape functions with neural networks.
Bound numerical error using finite element discretization error and network generalization error.
Reconstruct transition-matrix columns under linear displacement constraints to reproduce linear polynomial fields.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical experiments verify the theoretical results and demonstrate optimal convergence rates, good generalization performance, and numerical stability.
infographic.watch_item: Rigid-body displacement invariance alone does not guarantee convergence; implementation must enforce linear completeness, and error still depends on network generalization.
infographic.paper_title: Convergence and error analysis of problem-independent machine learning (PIML) with linear completeness

title: OAT3D: A Generative Model for 3D Shape- and Resolution-Free Structural Topology Optimization
authors: Hongrui Chen, Kittipong Thiamchaiboonthawee, Zhen Wei, Amin Heyrani Nobari, Faez Ahmed
abstract: Topology optimization determines how material should be distributed within a design domain to optimize structural performance under prescribed loads, supports, and constraints. The problems are highly nonconvex, and conventional solvers require repeated finite element analyses, making high-resolution 3D topology optimization computationally expensive. Data-driven approaches face an additional bottleneck: generating training datasets requires solving large numbers of these costly problems, so existing work in data-driven topology optimization primarily focuses on 2D problems. Large-scale 3D datasets remain scarce, and existing models remain limited in problem scale and boundary-condition diversity. Here, we introduce Optimize Any Topology-3D (OAT3D), a generative model for high-resolution 3D structural topology optimization. OAT3D introduces a novel sparse problem encoding to represent load and fixity conditions and combines a sparse volumetric variational autoencoder with a conditional diffusion transformer. We construct a dataset of 501,865 optimized topologies, generated using 51,800 GPU-hours and encompassing structures with up to one million elements and substantially more complex loading and support configurations than any existing structural topology optimization dataset. To our knowledge, this is the largest dataset for 3D topology optimization structures. Trained on this dataset, OAT3D generates structures at 512$^3$ resolution and achieves a $44.9\times$ speedup for raw candidate structure generation or $3.65\times$ speedup to reach similar compliance over conventional topology optimization. These contributions expand the scale and diversity of data-driven topology optimization for three-dimensional structural design.

infographic.key_insight: OAT3D generates high-resolution 3D structural topologies using sparse representations and conditional diffusion, reducing reliance on costly iterative optimization.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The model could accelerate material-layout exploration for 3D structures under varied loads and supports.
method: Sparsely encode load and fixity conditions.
Represent structures with a sparse volumetric variational autoencoder.
Generate topologies with a conditional diffusion transformer.
infographic.evidence_signal: Trained on 501,865 optimized topologies generated using 51,800 GPU-hours, OAT3D produces structures at 512³ resolution and reports 44.9× faster raw candidate generation or 3.65× speedup to similar compliance versus conventional topology optimization.
infographic.watch_item: Raw generation speed does not imply equivalent structural performance; generated designs still require compliance and constraint verification.
infographic.paper_title: OAT3D: A Generative Model for 3D Shape- and Resolution-Free Structural Topology Optimization

title: Atomistic insight into defect-mediated boron redistribution and high-temperature strengthening in TiAl alloys
authors: Xiang Meng, Shuhei Shinzato, Zhiqiang Zhao, Linfeng Yu, Jian Guo, Liangli Chu
abstract: Boron (B) microalloying can effectively refine microstructures of as-cast TiAl alloys and regulate their mechanical properties. Yet, how dilute B exists in TiAl and interacts with defects and how these interactions govern high-temperature deformation remain elusive. Here, we systematically elucidate defect-mediated B redistribution in TiAl alloys and its consequences for their deformation using hybrid grand-canonical Monte Carlo/molecular dynamics simulations augmented with a newly developed high-fidelity machine-learning potential. As a typical product of B microalloying, borides are markedly stiffer than the TiAl matrix and act as brittle reinforcing phases, while borides/matrix interfacial adhesion depends on surface termination and stacking sequence. In the bulk, interstitial B tends to be trapped at Ti-rich octahedral sites by high migration barriers but can kinetically evolve into substitutional dopants upon approaching Al vacancies. Increased tensile stress and vacancy concentration further promote B enrichment in the bulk. B is enriched at semi-coherent $γ/α_2$ boundaries and preferentially partitions into the $α_2$ phase. In polycrystalline TiAl, B accumulates primarily in disordered regions, raising the average flow stress by 9.4% at 1 at.% B and 900 K. This strengthening is accompanied by reduced shear strain accumulation. Simulated microstructural evolution and stacking-fault energetics indicate that B impedes dislocation glide via local pinning and suppresses deformation twinning, thereby increasing resistance to plastic deformation. By linking solute redistribution to defect interactions and deformation, these findings establish an atomistic framework for understanding and designing high-performance alloys based on interstitial solutes.

infographic.key_insight: Boron redistributes toward defects in TiAl, pinning dislocations and suppressing deformation twinning to increase high-temperature strength.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Controlling boron content and defect populations could help engineers strengthen TiAl alloys while accounting for brittle boride phases and interface-dependent adhesion.
method: Developed a high-fidelity machine-learning interatomic potential.
Combined grand-canonical Monte Carlo and molecular dynamics simulations.
Analyzed boron segregation, defect interactions, and deformation mechanisms.
infographic.evidence_signal: Polycrystalline TiAl simulations showed a 9.4% increase in average flow stress at 1 at.% boron and 900 K, accompanied by reduced shear strain accumulation.
infographic.watch_item: The reported strengthening is simulation-based; experimental validation is needed to establish performance under practical processing and loading conditions.
infographic.paper_title: Atomistic insight into defect-mediated boron redistribution and high-temperature strengthening in TiAl alloys

title: Constrained Allen-Cahn phase-field topology optimization of flexoelectric devices
authors: Hao Zhen, Sheng Mao
abstract: Topology optimization provides an effective approach to exploring performance-oriented designs for miniature devices. In this work, a phase-field framework for constrained topology optimization of microscale flexoelectric devices is developed using a continuum model under the assumption of infinitesimal deformations. The material distribution is optimized at the device level with the output voltage as the objective. The framework also accommodates objectives based on capacitance or stored electrostatic energy. Manufacturing variations are incorporated through a worst-case objective over the prescribed geometric realizations, with spectral constraints imposed to maintain the structural connectivity. The framework is applied to two-dimensional pressure and bending sensors and a three-dimensional thin-film device. The optimized nominal output voltages reach approximately 4.8 times the initial value for the pressure sensor and 2.5-3.4 times the initial values for the bending sensors. The voltage gains arise primarily from increased mechanically induced source charge, with capacitance reduction providing an additional contribution that varies with the device configuration. Erosion analyses of representative designs further show that structural connectivity is well preserved when structural members become locally narrower, with the output voltage remaining close to that of the nominal configuration. Combined with specific microfabrication processes, this optimization framework is expected to provide a numerical basis for configuration screening and prototype development of flexoelectric devices.

infographic.key_insight: Constrained Allen–Cahn phase-field topology optimization boosts flexoelectric sensor voltage primarily by increasing mechanically induced source charge.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework supports performance-driven design of microscale flexoelectric devices while accounting for geometric manufacturing variations and structural connectivity.
method: Optimize material distribution using an infinitesimal-deformation continuum model and output voltage objective.
Account for manufacturing variations with a worst-case objective over prescribed geometric realizations.
Impose spectral constraints to preserve structural connectivity.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluations cover 2D pressure and bending sensors and a 3D thin-film device; nominal voltage gains reach approximately 4.8× for the pressure sensor and 2.5–3.4× for the bending sensors.
infographic.watch_item: Experimental validation and integration with specific microfabrication processes remain necessary to establish practical device performance.
infographic.paper_title: Constrained Allen-Cahn phase-field topology optimization of flexoelectric devices

title: A mixed-primal FEM for Poisson-Fermi interfacial problems
authors: Siyad Rahman Mandottil, Neela Nataraj, Ricardo Ruiz-Baier
abstract: This paper presents a mixed-primal FEM for a linearised Poisson--Fermi interface problem arising from the Bazant--Storey--Kornyshev theory, which describes electrostatic interactions in ionic solutions. It leads to a transmission problem coupling a fourth-order equation in the solvent region with a second-order equation in the solute region. To precisely compute the electrostatic stress and the interactive force in the electrolyte, we reformulate the fourth-order problem as a mixed system by introducing the gradient of the electrostatic potential, the divergence of its gradient, and the gradient of its divergence as additional independent variables. The second-order problem is studied in its primal form as this approach eliminates the requirement for Lagrange multipliers to enforce the transmission conditions. The resulting formulation is discretised using Raviart--Thomas finite elements for the vector variables and piecewise polynomial finite elements for the scalar variables. Well-posedness of the mixed-primal formulation and optimal a priori error estimates for the field variables as well as for the postprocessed Maxwell tensor are established under suitable regularity assumptions, in parameter-weighted norms in which the inf-sup constant is independent of the correlation length and of the permittivity ratio. The constants in the error estimates are independent of both parameters as well, up to a loss of at most half an order when the mesh does not resolve the length scale (square root of the relative permittivity); the Sobolev norms of the solution may still depend on the parameters through boundary layers. The postprocessed Maxwell stress converges with optimal order on quasi-uniform meshes, except for the lowest-order scheme in 3D. Numerical experiments validate the theoretical convergence rates and demonstrate the properties of the proposed method for problems in 2D and 3D.

infographic.key_insight: A mixed-primal FEM couples fourth-order solvent electrostatics with a second-order solute model while supporting accurate Maxwell stress recovery.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The method supports electrostatic stress and interaction-force calculations in ionic solutions with material interfaces.
method: Introduce auxiliary gradient and divergence fields to reformulate the fourth-order solvent equation.
Retain a primal solute formulation, avoiding Lagrange multipliers for transmission conditions.
Discretise vector fields with Raviart–Thomas elements and scalar fields with piecewise polynomials.
infographic.evidence_signal: Theoretical stability and error estimates are supported by 2D and 3D numerical experiments validating convergence rates.
infographic.watch_item: Unresolved parameter-dependent length scales can reduce convergence by up to half an order; lowest-order 3D Maxwell stress recovery is also an exception to optimal convergence.
infographic.paper_title: A mixed-primal FEM for Poisson-Fermi interfacial problems

title: PhysRF-WorldJEPA: Transforming Heterogeneous Large Language Models into Manifold-Decoupled Millimeter-Wave Radar World Models
authors: Yicheng Huang, Feng Ke, Linhan Chen, Ziyi Jiang, Xiu Yin Zhang
abstract: Adapting Large Language Models (LLMs) to millimeter-wave (mmWave) radar enables privacy-preserving, all-weather physical scene understanding across darkness, smoke, and walls. However, standard instruction tuning treats continuous radar streams as static text-like tokens, causing near-random global radar-to-text retrieval and severe physical drift under sensor blackouts. Conversely, coupling pairwise contrastive losses (e.g., SigLIP) directly into the shared backbone improves retrieval but injects $O(B^2)$ repulsive gradients that fracture continuous coordinate manifolds ($R^2 < 0$). We present PhysRF-WorldJEPA, a manifold-decoupled Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) that separates continuous electromagnetic state prediction from cross-modal language alignment. An unattenuated 1.0x clock anchor and parallel dual-scale RF encoder feed a lean ~3% LoRA LLM trained with two-step state-space EMA-JEPA (Denoise -> Rollout) and sample-axis Batch-VICReg to predict +3.0 s physical states; a stop-gradient alignment head then maps frozen prompt states onto the text hypersphere with false-negative masking. On a 4,541-window tri-domain suite (77/60.25/60 GHz) against 10 baselines, freezing the physical backbone and training only the decoupled head lifts R->T R@10 from 5.95% to 15.01% and improves MedRank from 107.0 to 60.0 while preserving identical physical readout: 3.37 deg ($R^2=+0.961$) blackout +3.0 s torso tilt, 1.89 m ($R^2=+0.679$; 1.19 m/+0.863 at the RF front-end) cluttered UAV altitude, 2.04 m ($R^2=+0.461$) behind-wall NLOS range, 0.9976 virtual-RIS invariance, and 100% fall recall. Across five 0.5B-1.8B LLM families (15 zero-overhead models), World-JEPA improves retrieval and 75%-drop completion in 10/10 runs and blackout tilt in 4/5 (Span-Euc), 2/5 (Scatter), and 5/5 (per-family best) over SFT.

infographic.key_insight: Separating radar-state prediction from language alignment improves radar-to-text retrieval without degrading continuous physical-state estimates.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Privacy-preserving mmWave sensing could support motion and scene monitoring through darkness, smoke, and walls, although fracture or material-damage assessment is not demonstrated.
method: Dual-scale RF encoder and ~3% LoRA-adapted LLM predict physical states 3 seconds ahead.
Two-step EMA-JEPA training combines denoising, rollout, and sample-axis Batch-VICReg.
A separate stop-gradient alignment head maps frozen physical representations to text with false-negative masking.
infographic.evidence_signal: On 4,541 radar windows across three domains against 10 baselines, head-only alignment increased radar-to-text R@10 from 5.95% to 15.01% while preserving physical readouts, including 3.37° blackout torso-tilt error at +3 seconds.
infographic.watch_item: Retrieval R@10 remains 15.01%, and transfer beyond the evaluated radar domains—including structural damage sensing—requires validation.
infographic.paper_title: PhysRF-WorldJEPA: Transforming Heterogeneous Large Language Models into Manifold-Decoupled Millimeter-Wave Radar World Models

title: HEAR, SEE, SPIKE ONCE: Highly Efficient NeuroAI Temporal Neural Networks for Low-Precision Multimodal Audio-Visual Classification and Online Learning
authors: Shanmuga Venkatachalam, Quinn Jacobson, John Paul Shen
abstract: Spiking neural networks for multimodal audio-visual classification reach high accuracy by adopting deep-learning machinery: multi-stage convolutional or transformer encoders trained end-to-end with surrogate-gradient backpropagation through time. These prior works typically rely on full-precision (32-bit) parameters and do not treat hardware efficiency as a primary design objective. In this paper, we propose NeuTNN-AV, a much simpler hardware-amenable multimodal substrate built on the recently proposed NeuroAI Temporal Neural Network (NeuTNN) and demonstrate that it can match or outperform state-of-the-art SNN baselines with a fraction of their synapse counts. NeuTNN neurons carry multiple active dendritic segments. Each input line spikes at most once (temporal coding) and every weight is learned via a local reward-modulated spike-timing dependent plasticity (STDP) rule. All weights are 4-bit integers and inference uses only comparisons and additions. On CREMA-D, it reaches 78.6% with 2.34M synapses establishing a new state-of-the-art SNN accuracy, against 77.14% for MISNet-XL (31M parameters). On UrbanSound8K-AV, NeuTNN reaches 98.82% with 1.38M synapses, against 96.85% for SMMT (9.99M parameters) and 98.96% for MISNet-XL (31M parameters). Weight memory is 23-106x smaller than the spiking baselines, and the measured synaptic energy per inference is two to three orders of magnitude lower. Furthermore, the proposed NeuTNN learns CREMA-D in a single pass with 73.8% accuracy and demonstrates rapid online continual learning by adapting to unseen actors from a few dozen clips.

infographic.key_insight: NeuTNN-AV achieves competitive multimodal audio-visual classification using 4-bit weights, local learning, and far fewer synapses than leading spiking baselines.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Its comparison-and-addition inference offers a hardware-efficient approach for resource-constrained audio-visual sensing, though solid-mechanics applications are not evaluated.
method: Encode inputs temporally, with each input line spiking at most once.
Use neurons with multiple active dendritic segments and local reward-modulated STDP learning.
Store weights as 4-bit integers and perform inference using only comparisons and additions.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports 78.6% accuracy on CREMA-D with 2.34M synapses and 98.82% on UrbanSound8K-AV with 1.38M synapses, alongside 23–106× smaller weight memory than spiking baselines.
infographic.watch_item: Reported energy savings concern synaptic operations; end-to-end hardware efficiency, including input processing, remains to be established.
infographic.paper_title: HEAR, SEE, SPIKE ONCE: Highly Efficient NeuroAI Temporal Neural Networks for Low-Precision Multimodal Audio-Visual Classification and Online Learning

title: Verifying the Outputs of PDE Solvers: From Finite Elements to Neural Surrogates
authors: Konstantinos Dovelos
abstract: Physics simulation outputs increasingly come from solvers that no expert inspects, such as third-party packages in automated pipelines, programs written by large language models (LLMs), and learned surrogates. In earlier work on cardiac pulsed field ablation, we proposed that solvers return a certificate with their answers. The certificate consists of an admissible potential and an exactly charge-conserving current, and a small independent checker turns it into guaranteed error bounds against a written specification of the physics. Here, the same checker verifies the outputs of other solvers on the same problem. Specifically, FEniCSx computes both fields and receives the same bounds as our own solver. Five plausible bugs in a correct solver, one of them about 0.2% from the true impedance, all converge and pass a grid convergence study, yet the certificate rejects or refutes all five. Of three solvers written by LLMs, one is correct and certified to 0.1%, and one never solves the equation but converges. Neural networks that predict the coefficients of a reduced basis emit admissible fields and receive valid per-prediction bounds, at most 0.0021% wide inside their training range and 0.3-25% wide outside it, where 90% conformal intervals cover none of 14 tests. Untuned Fourier neural operators with free nodal outputs receive valid but uninformative bounds. On a uniform grid, interpolation onto the certificate grid limits them, and on the certificate grid, thin cells turn small nodal errors into large energy errors. Energy-norm training narrows the certified interval tenfold, and projecting the nodal-loss outputs onto the reduced basis narrows it by two to four orders of magnitude, still uninformative. The guarantee concerns the stated model and holds for any output, wherever its input lies. It is informative only when the output is accurate in energy on a grid that resolves the problem.

infographic.key_insight: An independent certificate checker provides guaranteed error bounds for PDE solver outputs, including finite-element solutions and neural predictions, without trusting the solver.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Certificate-based verification can help engineers detect misleadingly converged simulations and assess surrogate predictions against a specified physics model.
method: Return an admissible potential and an exactly charge-conserving current with each prediction.
Use a small independent checker to compute guaranteed error bounds.
Apply the same checker to conventional, LLM-written, and neural solvers.
infographic.evidence_signal: The checker rejected or refuted five bugs that passed grid-convergence studies; reduced-basis neural predictions received bounds at most 0.0021% wide in-range and 0.3–25% wide out-of-range.
infographic.watch_item: Guarantees apply only to the stated model; informative bounds require energy-accurate outputs on a sufficiently resolving grid.
infographic.paper_title: Verifying the Outputs of PDE Solvers: From Finite Elements to Neural Surrogates

title: Topology-Prior-Guided Regional Latent Dynamics for Transient Structural Response Prediction
authors: Yuan Zhang, Mohammad Amin Nabian, Shaotong Fu, Yiding Liu, Chengcheng Chu, Xuelin Tao
abstract: Predicting the transient nonlinear responses of complex engineering structures remains challenging due to large finite element meshes, heterogeneous structural components, and history-dependent mechanical behavior. This study proposes a topology-prior-guided regional latent dynamics (TPLD) surrogate model that combines physically structured regional representations with dynamics-aware latent learning for full-field time-history prediction. Based on mesh topology and engineering priors, structural responses are encoded into spatially coupled regional latent variables through region-aware feature extraction and topology-constrained interactions. An auxiliary one-step prediction task enhances latent-space dynamical predictability by introducing state-transition supervision. A load-conditioned spatiotemporal Mamba model then predicts regional latent trajectories by integrating temporal causal scanning and bidirectional spatial scanning, while a shared coordinate-conditioned decoder reconstructs full-field nodal responses. The framework is evaluated on three finite element datasets: a parametric stiffened panel, a partitioned pressure impact plate, and a Toyota Yaris full-vehicle crash model. The relative L2 errors for the three displacement components range from 4.00% to 8.21% on the stiffened panel and from 1.41% to 12.22% on the approximately 1.49-million-node vehicle model. On the BIW crash benchmark, TPLD achieves a relative L2 position error of 0.620%, representing a 30.7% reduction compared with the best-performing GeoTransolver configuration. Ablation studies demonstrate the advantages of topology-guided regional representations over global latent and learnable soft-slice alternatives, while auxiliary one-step prediction particularly improves the prediction of accumulated plastic strain.

infographic.key_insight: Topology-guided regional latent dynamics enables accurate full-field transient structural response prediction while preserving spatial structure and learning history-dependent behavior.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach offers a surrogate for large nonlinear finite element simulations, including vehicle crash models with approximately 1.49 million nodes.
method: Encode responses into coupled regional latent states using mesh topology and engineering priors.
Use auxiliary one-step prediction to improve latent dynamical predictability.
Predict load-conditioned trajectories with spatiotemporal Mamba, then reconstruct nodal responses with a shared coordinate-conditioned decoder.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across three FEM datasets, displacement relative L2 errors ranged from 4.00–8.21% for the stiffened panel and 1.41–12.22% for the vehicle model; BIW position error was 0.620%, a 30.7% reduction versus the best-performing GeoTransolver configuration.
infographic.watch_item: Performance on unseen geometries, topologies, or loading regimes is not established by the abstract and requires validation.
infographic.paper_title: Topology-Prior-Guided Regional Latent Dynamics for Transient Structural Response Prediction

title: A geometric-IEQ approach for curvature-driven flows
authors: Harald Garcke, Yifei Li, Robert Nürnberg, Quan Zhao
abstract: We introduce a geometric invariant energy quadratization (IEQ) formulation for the $L^2$-gradient flow of a class of curvature-dependent energies of closed hypersurfaces, where the energy density depends on the mean curvature and the unit normal. A square-root auxiliary variable converts the geometric energy into a quadratic functional. Combining its evolution equation with a skew-symmetric treatment of surface transport yields a weak formulation whose energy law depends only on the normal velocity and is therefore independent of the chosen tangential motion. We construct monolithic nonlinear parametric finite element methods by coupling a common IEQ discretization with one of two geometric formulations that accommodate either the Barrett-Garcke-Nürnberg (BGN) tangential velocity or the minimal-deformation-rate (MDR) tangential velocity. Both fully discrete approximations satisfy an unconditional decay estimate for the discrete quadratic energy. We further extend the construction to anisotropic Willmore flow, and to $H^{-1}$-gradient flows. A variety of numerical experiments are presented to demonstrate the robustness and accuracy of the introduced methods.

infographic.key_insight: A geometric invariant energy quadratization (IEQ) formulation enables curvature-driven surface evolution with unconditional discrete energy decay, independent of tangential motion.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach supports energy-stable finite element simulation of curvature-driven interface evolution, including anisotropic Willmore and H⁻¹-gradient flows.
method: Introduce a square-root auxiliary variable to express the geometric energy as a quadratic functional.
Use skew-symmetric surface transport so the energy law depends only on normal velocity.
Couple the IEQ discretization to monolithic nonlinear parametric FEM with BGN or minimal-deformation-rate tangential motion.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports numerical experiments demonstrating robustness and accuracy, but provides no quantitative errors or runtime comparisons.
infographic.watch_item: Unconditional energy decay does not eliminate nonlinear solver costs or time-step accuracy concerns; this is a numerical FEM method, not an AI surrogate.
infographic.paper_title: A geometric-IEQ approach for curvature-driven flows

title: Sparse Constitutive Neural Networks for Hyperelasticity
authors: Hendrik Geisler, Clément Jailin, Emmanuel Baranger
abstract: Constitutive model identification aims to recover compact, interpretable models that accurately describe material behavior. In this work, we identify hyperelastic constitutive models using artificial neural networks with sparsity-promoting constraints and regularization. The proposed method combines the expressiveness of neural networks with the structural interpretability of sparse constitutive models, such as those identified by EUCLID, by representing the strain energy density as a sum of products of univariate functions of the invariants. The resulting decomposition exposes the contributions of individual invariants and their interactions. The method is demonstrated on synthetic data in supervised and unsupervised learning scenarios, showing that it can accurately identify interpretable constitutive models with few active modes.

infographic.key_insight: Sparse neural networks identify compact hyperelastic strain-energy models while exposing individual invariant contributions and their interactions.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach supports interpretable material-model identification for solid mechanics simulations.
method: Represent strain-energy density as a sum of products of univariate functions of invariants.
Apply sparsity-promoting constraints and regularization to retain few active modes.
Identify constitutive models in supervised and unsupervised learning settings.
infographic.evidence_signal: Synthetic-data demonstrations in both learning settings show accurate, interpretable constitutive models with few active modes.
infographic.watch_item: Validation on noisy experimental data and generalization beyond the tested loading conditions remain unestablished by the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Sparse Constitutive Neural Networks for Hyperelasticity

title: A decoupled BDF2-type integrator for the spin-diffusion Landau--Lifshitz--Gilbert system in ferromagnetic multilayers
authors: Michele Aldé, Dirk Praetorius, Agus L. Soenjaya
abstract: We propose and analyze a fully discrete, linear, decoupled BDF2-type finite element integrator for the spin-diffusion Landau--Lifshitz--Gilbert (SDLLG) system arising in spintronics. The SDLLG equations couple the magnetization dynamics with a diffusion equation for spin accumulation. The proposed numerical method combines a projection-free BDF2-type tangent-plane discretization of the magnetization dynamics with BDF2 time-stepping for the spin accumulation. By treating the coupling terms explicitly through extrapolation, each time step requires only two independent linear solves that can be performed in parallel. The analysis accommodates the usual exchange field and a general, possibly nonlinear, lower-order effective field. Unconditional weak convergence towards a global weak solution is shown. We also establish bounds on the deviation from the unit-length constraint. Under additional assumptions on the associated energy functional, an energy inequality for the limiting solution is obtained. Numerical experiments support the theoretical findings.

infographic.key_insight: A linear, decoupled BDF2-type finite element integrator advances coupled magnetization and spin diffusion using two independent linear solves per time step.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The method supports parallel time-step solves for spin-transport and magnetization simulations in ferromagnetic multilayer spintronic devices.
method: Projection-free BDF2-type tangent-plane discretization for magnetization.
BDF2 time-stepping for spin accumulation.
Explicit extrapolation of coupling terms enables independent linear solves.
infographic.evidence_signal: The authors prove unconditional weak convergence and bounds on unit-length constraint deviation, with numerical experiments supporting the theoretical findings.
infographic.watch_item: Magnetization length is not enforced exactly, and the limiting energy inequality requires additional assumptions on the energy functional.
infographic.paper_title: A decoupled BDF2-type integrator for the spin-diffusion Landau--Lifshitz--Gilbert system in ferromagnetic multilayers

title: Efficient Optimization of Mechanical Metamaterials via Transferable Representation Learning
authors: Antonio Varagnolo, Miaomiao Dai, Bolei Deng, Raphaël Pestourie
abstract: Designing mechanical metamaterials for nonlinear behavior such as energy absorption is limited by high-dimensional parametrizations and by expensive simulations. Here we show that design knowledge from a cheap linear property can be transferred to nonlinear, potentially non-differentiable, targets through a learned, reusable search space. TRAMA (TRAnsferable representation learning for Metamaterial Architectures) reparametrizes architected materials using a variational autoencoder with a pre-trained vision transformer and physics-informed augmentations. For energy-absorption efficiency, TRAMA reaches every efficiency level with 95 to 98% reduction in the evaluations needed by state-of-the-art gradient-free optimization and 3 to 5 fewer than gradient-based optimization. Its best design is comparable to the best found by any baseline with at least 67% fewer evaluations, which translate into approximately 100 hours saved per campaign with finite-element simulations. Fabricated designs match simulated stress-strain curves within 5.3%. A post hoc analysis shows where the representation transfers to new properties and where it does not.

infographic.key_insight: TRAMA transfers knowledge from a cheap linear property into a reusable learned search space for optimizing nonlinear mechanical metamaterial behavior.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach reduces expensive simulation calls for energy-absorbing metamaterial design, saving approximately 100 hours per finite-element optimization campaign.
method: Learn a compact design representation using a variational autoencoder.
Incorporate a pre-trained vision transformer and physics-informed augmentations.
Reuse the learned search space to optimize nonlinear, potentially non-differentiable targets.
infographic.evidence_signal: For energy-absorption efficiency, TRAMA required 95–98% fewer evaluations than state-of-the-art gradient-free optimization; fabricated designs matched simulated stress–strain curves within 5.3%.
infographic.watch_item: Transferability is property-dependent: the learned representation does not generalize equally well to every new target.
infographic.paper_title: Efficient Optimization of Mechanical Metamaterials via Transferable Representation Learning

title: Load Balancing Neurons: Firing-Rate Control Sustains Plasticity in Continual Learning
authors: Jan Robine, Marc Höftmann, Stefan Harmeling
abstract: Neural networks in continual learning often lose plasticity: some neurons become inactive, while others fire almost constantly. This limits adaptation to shifting data and wastes capacity. Prior work mitigates this by periodically reinitializing low-utility units, but such resets can destroy previously learned features and do not proactively prevent low utility. We study a simple diagnostic measure: the firing rate of ReLU units, defined as the fraction of positive pre-activations. Low rates identify dead units, while very high rates indicate linearized, always-on units. Based on this view, we introduce a lightweight load-balancing mechanism that adjusts per-neuron thresholds to keep firing rates within a target range. Across continual ImageNet and class-incremental CIFAR-100, firing-rate distributions explain differences in plasticity across a range of approaches, including well-known techniques such as L2 regularization and non-affine normalization, and load balancing matches or exceeds reset-based methods on both benchmarks. The same mechanism carries over to reinforcement learning, improving Rainbow DQN on Atari over a LayerNorm baseline.

infographic.key_insight: Keeping ReLU firing rates within a target range helps prevent inactive and always-on neurons, sustaining plasticity during continual learning.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This approach may help engineering models adapt to changing data, though the abstract reports no solid-mechanics validation.
method: Measure each ReLU neuron's firing rate as the fraction of positive pre-activations.
Adjust per-neuron thresholds to keep firing rates within a target range.
Balance neuron activity without periodically reinitializing learned units.
infographic.evidence_signal: Load balancing matches or exceeds reset-based methods on continual ImageNet and class-incremental CIFAR-100, and improves Rainbow DQN on Atari over a LayerNorm baseline.
infographic.watch_item: Target firing-rate ranges and threshold-update settings require implementation choices whose sensitivity is not specified in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Load Balancing Neurons: Firing-Rate Control Sustains Plasticity in Continual Learning

title: AI agents can redesign engineering parts with more than a thousand CAD parameters and nonlinear simulations
authors: Alexandra Starostina, Alexander Hermann, Mahish Guru, Kartik Bali, Roland Aydin, Christian C. Cyron
abstract: Simulation-driven design of real engineering components has to meet three conditions at once. It runs on few solves, since a nonlinear finite-element simulation of a 3D part takes hours; its design space has many values, the hundreds to thousands of values of the part's CAD model; and a better design often needs a redesign, coordinated changes of the part's proportions rather than local polishing of its surface. Automated optimisers meet at most two of these conditions. Classical optimisers, Bayesian or derivative-free, need a person to cut the design down to a few parameters, and on all the values they need far more solves; industrial shape optimisers move every surface node of the mesh in one solve per cycle, but only in small steps that polish rather than redesign. We ask whether a general-purpose large language model (LLM) can meet all three by joining what it knows with what the simulation shows. GPT-6 Astra edits a magnesium stent through a CAD geometry parametrisation of about 1,650 values, with a budget of 15 simulations; every proposal is built in CAD, meshed and simulated with large-deformation plasticity and contact, and the LLM reads the full results of every solve. Within that budget it lowered the objective, a high percentile of the strains in the stent's bends, by 32%; on the same budget, the industrial shape optimiser Tosca improved the original design by a tenth and then stopped improving. An earlier GPT-6 Astra design, 25% lower in the same objective, was checked in an independent, higher-fidelity model of the full deployment with crimping and damage: it was 14% less strained than the original after the full chain, and its most damaged spot began to fail later and carried 63% less damage at full expansion. LLMs can thus join their learned knowledge with simulation data to adjust more than a thousand design values and reach valid designs with real improvements.

infographic.key_insight: An LLM agent coordinated changes across about 1,650 CAD parameters to reduce a magnesium stent’s high-percentile bend strain by 32% within 15 nonlinear simulations.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Simulation-guided AI could enable substantial component redesign when nonlinear finite-element solves are costly and the CAD design space is large.
method: GPT-6 Astra proposed edits to the stent’s CAD geometry.
Each proposal was built, meshed and simulated with large-deformation plasticity and contact.
The agent used full simulation results to guide subsequent edits.
infographic.evidence_signal: Under the same 15-simulation budget, Tosca improved the objective by about 10%; an earlier AI design independently evaluated through full deployment showed 14% lower strain and 63% less damage at the most damaged spot.
infographic.watch_item: Evidence is limited to one component, and the independent higher-fidelity validation tested an earlier design rather than the final 32%-improved design.
infographic.paper_title: AI agents can redesign engineering parts with more than a thousand CAD parameters and nonlinear simulations

title: Uncertainty Quantification and Global Sensitivity Analysis of Patient-Specific Coronary Hemodynamics Under Unsteady Flow Conditions
authors: Muhammad Usman, Nafis M. Arefin, Akil Narayan, Lucas H. Timmins
abstract: Patient-specific computational models of the coronary arteries demonstrate transformative potential for physiological assessment, identifying hemodynamic markers associated with disease progression, and optimizing treatment. Unfortunately, these models rarely account for input parameter uncertainty, limiting confidence in predictions and their clinical interpretation. Herein, we present a novel uncertainty quantification-finite element framework that integrates computationally efficient techniques to characterize and propagate uncertainty through patient-specific coronary simulations under unsteady flow conditions. Principal component analysis characterized variability in pulsatile coronary velocity waveforms, while uncertainty in blood pressure, viscosity, density, and heart rate is represented through probability distributions. Polynomial chaos expansion (PCE) enabled efficient uncertainty propagation and global sensitivity analysis across three patient-specific models, quantifying variability in time-averaged wall shear stress (WSS), oscillatory shear index, and cross-flow index. Fourth-order PCE emulators converged across all three patients, yielding analyses of 505 models per patient, with median coefficients of variation ranging from 0.15-0.20 for time-averaged WSS, 0.54-0.75 for oscillatory shear index, and 0.28-0.38 for cross-flow index, highlighting greater relative uncertainty in multidirectional WSS metrics. Global sensitivity analysis revealed that time-averaged WSS variability was governed by the individual effects of velocity and blood viscosity, with parameter interactions contributing <2% of total variance. In contrast, velocity waveform uncertainty dominated variability in the oscillatory shear index and cross-flow index, with higher-order parameter interactions accounting for 20.7-34.5% and 26.6-37.8% of total variance, respectively.

infographic.key_insight: Uncertainty in pulsatile coronary flow affects oscillatory and multidirectional wall-shear metrics more strongly than time-averaged wall shear stress.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Quantifying input uncertainty can help contextualize patient-specific coronary hemodynamic predictions and prioritize measurements that reduce prediction variability.
method: Use principal component analysis to characterize velocity-waveform variability.
Propagate uncertain velocity, pressure, viscosity, density, and heart rate through unsteady finite-element simulations using polynomial chaos expansion.
Apply global sensitivity analysis to separate individual parameter effects from interactions.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across three patient-specific geometries and 505 models per patient, fourth-order PCE emulators converged; median coefficients of variation were 0.15–0.20 for time-averaged WSS, 0.54–0.75 for oscillatory shear index, and 0.28–0.38 for cross-flow index.
infographic.watch_item: Evaluation covered only three patients; broader generalizability and clinical predictive accuracy remain unestablished in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Uncertainty Quantification and Global Sensitivity Analysis of Patient-Specific Coronary Hemodynamics Under Unsteady Flow Conditions

title: Reliable and grounded reporting of any computed tomography scan with FORA
authors: Sezgin Er, Utku Turkbey, Alperen Gur, Omer Faruk Durugol, Suprosanna Shit, Murong Xu
abstract: Artificial intelligence systems for computed tomography (CT) remain largely restricted to specific anatomical regions, examination types or predefined abnormalities, limiting their ability to provide comprehensive and spatially grounded interpretations. Here we present FORA, a general-purpose CT model that recognizes and spatially localizes 1,028 hierarchically organized radiological concepts and generates reports across the 28 CT protocols represented in our cohort. Trained on 304,962 routine CT examinations supervised by their accompanying reports, FORA learns to localize abnormalities without manually annotated lesions. Its architecture combines multiple-instance learning with an interpretable concept bottleneck that connects spatial evidence, radiological findings and report generation. We first developed and benchmarked the architecture on chest radiographs, achieving state-of-the-art performance, before training a separate model on three-dimensional CT examinations. On 36,619 held-out CT examinations, FORA achieved a macro area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.918 for radiological concept recognition, exceeding the strongest of 18 existing CT models by 0.21. FORA also ranked first on three public benchmarks, outperforming Merlin on its own test set without training on that institution's data (AUROC 0.907 versus 0.826). On independent localization benchmarks for pulmonary emboli, renal masses and rib fractures, FORA's strongest spatial evidence fell within annotated lesions at rates up to 348 times greater than chance. FORA achieved more than threefold higher macro-averaged finding recall than the strongest existing report generator. These results show that a single model can combine broad abnormality recognition, spatial localization and report generation across 12 CT examination types, using routine reports without lesion-level supervision.

infographic.key_insight: FORA combines recognition of 1,028 radiological concepts, spatial localization and CT report generation in one model trained without manually annotated lesions.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For computational imaging and fracture assessment, FORA demonstrates report-supervised localization of findings such as rib fractures, rather than mechanical damage prediction.
method: Train on 304,962 routine CT examinations paired with radiology reports.
Use multiple-instance learning to localize abnormalities without lesion-level supervision.
Connect spatial evidence to findings and report generation through an interpretable concept bottleneck.
infographic.evidence_signal: On 36,619 held-out CT examinations, FORA achieved 0.918 macro AUROC for concept recognition; independent localization tests showed lesion-hit rates up to 348 times chance.
infographic.watch_item: Clinical deployment requires further validation beyond the represented CT protocols; strong recognition and localization do not by themselves establish report safety.
infographic.paper_title: Reliable and grounded reporting of any computed tomography scan with FORA

title: DED-Agent: An agentic AI method for autonomous thermal simulation model development and calibration in laser directed energy deposition
authors: Michael Song, Yilong Dai, Lin Cheng
abstract: In metal additive manufacturing (AM), process parameters set the local thermal history, which governs defects, microstructure and properties. Laser power, scan speed, hatch spacing, layer thickness, scan strategy and position combine into a design space of 10^4-10^6 conditions, which is beyond what human experts can map by hand with finite element (FE) thermal models: every model must be set up, meshed, solved and calibrated by an expert, and calibrating unknown heat-source parameters alone can take days to weeks. This paper presents DED-Agent, an agentic artificial intelligence (AI) method for autonomous simulation model development and calibration in laser directed energy deposition (L-DED). A supervisor agent coordinates three specialist agents that share a structured simulation specification and call open-source tools. An intent agent turns a plain-language request into a validated specification, a simulation agent builds, runs and checks an FE thermal model through physics-aware step-by-step reasoning, and a calibration agent identifies key heat-source parameters against experimental data (e.g., thermocouple data) using a high-order proper generalized decomposition (HOPGD) surrogate within a trust-region search. On five benchmark builds, from single-track walls to a multi-track band on a cylindrical tube, the agents built executable thermal models without manual intervention, with 4.1-9.1% error for the simple and medium builds. Within three calibration rounds, the error fell to 0.9-2.5%. The surrogate matched full FE to within 0.08-1.55% and shortened calibration by 5-13 times. Agentic AI can thus autonomously establish reliable, accurate simulation models for AM processes and accelerate the search for process parameters that control microstructure.

infographic.key_insight: DED-Agent autonomously builds and calibrates laser directed energy deposition thermal FE models, combining coordinated AI agents with surrogate-assisted parameter search.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Automating thermal model setup and calibration can accelerate exploration of additive manufacturing parameters that influence defects, microstructure and properties.
method: A supervisor coordinates intent, simulation and calibration agents through a shared structured specification.
Agents translate plain-language requests into validated specifications, then build, run and check thermal FE models using open-source tools.
Calibration fits heat-source parameters to experimental data using a high-order proper generalized decomposition surrogate within a trust-region search.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across five benchmark builds, models ran without manual intervention; simple and medium builds had 4.1–9.1% initial error, reduced to 0.9–2.5% within three calibration rounds, while surrogate errors were 0.08–1.55% and calibration was 5–13× faster.
infographic.watch_item: Validation covers five benchmark builds; reliability for broader geometries, materials and process regimes remains to be established.
infographic.paper_title: DED-Agent: An agentic AI method for autonomous thermal simulation model development and calibration in laser directed energy deposition

title: Stabilized Isogeometric Topology Optimization on Trimmed Geometries
authors: Haoyu Su, Giuliano Guarino, Xiaodong Wei
abstract: This paper presents a novel stabilized isogeometric topology optimization method for complex design domains represented by trimmed geometries. Minimum compliance is taken as the model problem, where a generalized Cahn-Hilliard model, a time-dependent fourth-order partial differential equation, is solved and its steady-state solutions yield the optimized structures. This approach does not require sensitivity analysis and can naturally accommodate material constraints and complex topological changes. To impose Dirichlet boundary conditions and solve the instability issue caused by trimming, Nitsche's formulation with minimal stabilization is proposed for the high-order problem. Moreover, the immersed boundary-conformal method is extended to handle complex non-design domains, allowing material-void interfaces to be treated in a unified manner. Finally, a three-dimensional biharmonic problem and several two-dimensional topology optimization examples are presented to demonstrate the effectiveness, stability, and flexibility of the proposed method in dealing with complex design domains.

infographic.key_insight: Stabilized isogeometric topology optimization combines trimmed geometry representations with a generalized Cahn–Hilliard model to optimize structures without sensitivity analysis.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The method supports minimum-compliance structural design on complex domains while accommodating material constraints, topology changes, and non-design regions.
method: Evolve a fourth-order generalized Cahn–Hilliard PDE toward steady-state optimized structures.
Apply Nitsche’s formulation with minimal stabilization to impose Dirichlet conditions and address trimming-induced instability.
Extend the immersed boundary-conformal method to complex non-design domains and unified material–void interface treatment.
infographic.evidence_signal: A three-dimensional biharmonic problem and several two-dimensional topology optimization examples demonstrate effectiveness, stability, and geometric flexibility.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not establish three-dimensional topology optimization performance or computational scaling.
infographic.paper_title: Stabilized Isogeometric Topology Optimization on Trimmed Geometries
